questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the real, durable output of a purple team exercise?
options: A detailed slide deck summarizing which techniques were attempted
New or tuned detection logic actually running in the SIEM
A list of red team operator certifications earned during the exercise
A signed Rules of Engagement document
questions.explain: A finding that stays a bullet point in a report has changed nothing about tomorrow's detection capability. A deployed analytics rule actually has.

questions.q: In the example KQL query for detecting LSASS memory dumping, why does it exclude known EDR service accounts?
options: To comply with a legal requirement around credential access monitoring
To cut obvious false positives before the rule ships as a production analytics rule
Because EDR service accounts are never allowed to touch LSASS under any circumstances
To reduce the number of columns returned by the query
questions.explain: Excluding the organization's own known EDR service accounts removes an obvious source of false positives before the detection rule is trusted in production.

questions.q: Put these detection engineering lifecycle steps in the order this lesson describes them: deploy, build the query, test against the real technique, tune for false positives.
options: Deploy, build the query, tune for false positives, test against the real technique
Tune for false positives, deploy, build the query, test against the real technique
Test against the real technique, deploy, tune for false positives, build the query
Build the query, test against the real technique, tune for false positives, deploy
questions.explain: The lifecycle runs hypothesis, build, test against the real technique, tune for false-positive rate, deploy, then document — in that order.

questions.q: Besides new SIEM detection rules, what other real outputs can a purple team exercise produce, per this lesson?
options: A missing telemetry source being added, an EDR prevention policy update, or a SOAR playbook update
A reduction in the organization's total headcount
A permanent ban on all future red team engagements
Removal of the MITRE ATT&CK framework from future exercises
questions.explain: Gaps can also point to a missing telemetry source, a prevention policy that should auto-block the behavior, or an automated SOAR response — not only a new detection rule.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a single purple team exercise isn't enough on its own?
options: Because MITRE retires the ATT&CK framework and replaces it every year
Because regulations require a new exercise be run for every employee hired
Because detection coverage can quietly decay over time as environments, telemetry, and configurations change
Because red team operators are only certified to participate once
questions.explain: A rule that worked six months ago can silently stop firing as environments change, which is why mature programs run exercises on a recurring cadence and track coverage over time.
